name: Closed centre (d4-e5 chain against d5-e6)

plans.label: Land a kingside pawn on the fifth with the chain intact
plans.description: The e5 pawn faces the kingside: gain space there, reroute pieces behind the chain head, and get a pawn to f5, g5 or h5 while the centre stays shut.

success.note: RESTATED PLAN. The plan was 'Attack where the chain points', whose success was whether the storm was sound. It is now whether the storm arrived with the centre still shut: a White pawn on f5, g5 or h5 while d4 and e5 still stand. Overextension satisfies this census too. Original success note: 'No rules-arithmetic signature distinguishes attack from overextension.'

plans.label: Keep at least as many defenders on d4 as attackers
plans.description: Meet the strike at d4 with the c-pawn's support: the base still stands and White's defender count on it is at least equal to Black's pressure.

success.note: RESTATED PLAN. The plan was 'Hold the base', whose success was duration. It is now the count the plan itself names, read at one position: the d4 pawn still stands, Black is actually bearing on it, and White's defenders are at least as many as Black's attackers. The vocabulary has no operator comparing two counts, so the comparison is written out by case over the attainable range one to four or more — which makes it exact rather than a threshold guess. It says the count is held now; it cannot say it was held throughout. Original success note: 'Holding is duration, not a property one position can certify.'

plans.label: Strike the base with the c-pawn
plans.description: Hit the chain at its base, not its head: the c-pawn strike opens the c-file and keeps pressure on d4 after the trade.

success.note: The c-file opened for Black while the chain still stands and its base remains the target.

plans.label: Remove the chain head from e5
plans.description: Once the king is safe, the f-pawn strike undermines the chain head: White's e5 pawn is gone while the d4/d5 pair still stands.

success.note: RESTATED PLAN. The plan was 'Chip the head with the f-pawn', whose success was declined because the resulting structures vary. It is now the one fact all of them share: the chain head no longer stands on e5, while d4 and d5 still do. Original success note: 'The head trade resolves into too many shapes for one expression.'

watch: The attacker and defender counts on d4 as the file pressure builds.
Whether the f-pawn strike arrives before the base falls.
Which bishop is buried behind its own chain and whether it can be traded.
typicalMistakes: Attacking the chain's head before its base is under pressure.
Opening the side of the board where the opponent's chain points.
Trading the entombed bishop's problem away one tempo too late, or freeing the position for the opponent by timing a strike badly.

Trigger narrowing: the family spans every locked-chain orientation; this entry encodes only the d4-e5 versus d5-e6 interlock (French and Caro-Kann Advance shape). The mirrored e4-d5 versus e5-d6 chain (King's Indian and Benoni shape) and longer chains do not fire; encoding them honestly requires either a second entry with the plan sides reversed or a chain predicate the vocabulary lacks.
